reason: Re-opened packet.js gita 18 --verse 18.66 and found both readings at the place named. Madhva (Subba Rau, the 'V.' paragraph, which sources/vedanta.js confirms is the comment) says verbatim that abandoning all duties outright would be inconsistent with the teaching and the close of the work, that Krishna could not then urge Arjuna to fight, and that the phrase means abandoning the fruits of duties and the duties not meant for the delight of the Lord. Sastri's Sankara on 18.66 says dharma here includes adharma because naishkarmya is taught, so the passage means renouncing all works. Both paraphrases hold without drift, both schools are named, the two differ and the difference is not resolved, verse.js ok (18.66, at 687, 18 words) and entry-check ok (58 words). The attack that lands is the plain sense. 'Gives Arjuna a last charge' claims more than day.js carries: 18.67 is itself a further charge laid on Arjuna ('Never is this to be spoken by thee to anyone who is without asceticism'), so 18.66 is not his last charge, and 'last' is not the passage's own term. 18.64 calls it 'My supreme word, most secret of all', so the context can be said in the text's own words. A lesser point for the operator: as the verdict notes, recheck-evidence.js will report the evidence NOT FOUND on day 18 until its tag squash is fixed or a ruling is made, because of a stray '<' in the Sankara text on 18.9. The rewrite below passes entry-check, with no errors and no warnings, at 59 words.
better: Krishna, after promising Arjuna his supreme word, most secret of all, speaks it; Madhva (Dvaita), on 18.66, reads the abandoning as giving up the fruits of duty and any duty not done to please the Lord, since Krishna could not otherwise urge Arjuna to fight, and Śaṅkara (Advaita), on 18.66, as renouncing all works, unrighteous as well as righteous.
